title: Occupancy of Non‐Ice Environments Is Associated With Molt Disruption in the Leopard Seal
content:
ABSTRACT

Annual life-history events are sensitive to environmental conditions and individual health. In wide-ranging species spanning diverse habitats and climates, quantifying variation in those events can reveal an organism's sensitivity to ecological change. Leopard seals (Hydrurga leptonyx), unusual among Antarctic phocids in occupying both pack-ice and temperate coastlines, may help predict how ice-associated seals respond to a warming climate. Using 4066 photographs taken between 23.06°S and 75.51°S, we characterized leopard seal molt and identified two active molt types: (1) Immediate active molt- well-developed new hair replaced old hair concurrently and (2) Delayed active molt- hair loss initially revealed black skin or underdeveloped hair. Testing environmental variables, season, and indicators of poor health, generalized linear modeling and random forest classification identified environment type (ice vs. non-ice) and season as the strongest predictors of active molt type. Immediate active molt was associated with ice environments (98%), summer (88%), and the standard molt pattern. Delayed active molt was associated with non-ice environments (91%), spring (51%), standard and reverse patterns, and poor health. We conclude that immediate active molt represents the species' expected molt, whereas delayed active molt is a maladaptive consequence of occupying non-ice environments, a concern as climate change degrades ice habitats.
